docs.text: Lunar-gravity flame data now exists, outside PSI. docs.title: Q01 · Does the minimum oxygen concentration that supports flame spread fall below both its 0 g and 1 g values at lunar gravity?
docs.text: Does the minimum oxygen concentration that supports flame spread fall below both its 0 g and 1 g values at lunar gravity? Lunar habitats will be screened with 1 g tests. If lunar gravity is the most flammable condition, 1 g screening is not conservative. No long-duration measurement of the oxygen limit at 0.16 g for any material.

docs.title: Q02 · Why did SIBAL spread more slowly at lunar gravity than at 1 g in LUCI, yet keep burning about 45 seconds longer?
docs.text: Why did SIBAL spread more slowly at lunar gravity than at 1 g in LUCI, yet keep burning about 45 seconds longer? Slower spread but longer burning could mean a longer window for a fire to reach other materials. One flight, one sample per material, and a rotating platform with Coriolis effects.

docs.title: Q03 · At lunar gravity, does a flame spread faster against the airflow or with it, as it does in 0 g?
docs.text: At lunar gravity, does a flame spread faster against the airflow or with it, as it does in 0 g? Habitats have ventilation and gravity at once. Which spread direction dominates decides where detectors and fuel-free zones belong. No measurement combining forced ventilation with partial gravity.

docs.title: Q04 · At what gravity level does buoyancy alone supply enough oxygen to keep a flame alive without ventilation?
docs.text: At what gravity level does buoyancy alone supply enough oxygen to keep a flame alive without ventilation? If ventilation fails in a lunar habitat, will an existing fire starve or keep going? The gravity level where quiescent burning becomes self-sustaining is unknown.

docs.title: Q05 · Are Mars habitats (0.38 g) more or less flammable than lunar ones?
docs.text: Are Mars habitats (0.38 g) more or less flammable than lunar ones? Mars missions will need their own material screening rules. Thick materials, habitat atmospheres and burns longer than about 25 s at 0.38 g.

docs.title: Q06 · How long must a partial-gravity burn last for a thick material to reach steady spread?
docs.text: How long must a partial-gravity burn last for a thick material to reach steady spread? Short tests can mistake a flame that is still growing, or still dying, for a steady one. No partial-gravity platform has run long enough for thick fuels.

docs.title: Q07 · Can the 1 g Test 1 result be corrected to predict flammability at lunar gravity?
docs.text: Can the 1 g Test 1 result be corrected to predict flammability at lunar gravity? A correction factor would let existing Test 1 databases serve lunar missions. No paired Test 1 / lunar-gravity data set exists to fit a correction.

docs.title: Q08 · Do droplet extinction and cool flames behave differently at partial gravity?
docs.text: Do droplet extinction and cool flames behave differently at partial gravity? Liquid spills (fuels, solvents, lubricants) are a habitat hazard alongside solids. No droplet or cool-flame measurement between 0 g and 1 g.

docs.title: Q09 · Do the microgravity extinction limits measured for PMMA and SIBAL still hold at about 30% oxygen and 70 kPa?
docs.text: Do the microgravity extinction limits measured for PMMA and SIBAL still hold at about 30% oxygen and 70 kPa? This is the atmosphere planned for a lunar habitat. No mapping of extinction limits (oxygen vs airflow) at habitat conditions.

docs.title: Q10 · Is oxygen partial pressure or oxygen fraction the better predictor of flammability at reduced pressure in microgravity?
docs.text: Is oxygen partial pressure or oxygen fraction the better predictor of flammability at reduced pressure in microgravity? Habitats raise the oxygen fraction while lowering pressure; which of the two controls risk decides the safe operating envelope. Solids at matched partial pressure but different total pressure.

docs.title: Q11 · How does solid flame spread change with pressure when the oxygen fraction is held fixed?
docs.text: How does solid flame spread change with pressure when the oxygen fraction is held fixed? Separates the effect of pressure from the effect of oxygen, which current flight data mixes. No flight series varies pressure alone.

docs.title: Q12 · What is the lowest oxygen level at which PMMA sustains a flame in microgravity, across the full range of airflow?
docs.text: What is the lowest oxygen level at which PMMA sustains a flame in microgravity, across the full range of airflow? Defines how far oxygen must drop before a cabin fire cannot survive. The limit has not been mapped against airflow for flat PMMA, only for rods at a few flows.

docs.title: Q13 · Does Nomex stay non-flammable in a 30% oxygen, 70 kPa habitat atmosphere?
docs.text: Does Nomex stay non-flammable in a 30% oxygen, 70 kPa habitat atmosphere? Nomex is used for crew clothing and covers; its safety margin at habitat oxygen is unknown. No Nomex test above 22.2% oxygen.

docs.title: Q14 · How do diluents other than nitrogen change solid flammability?
docs.text: How do diluents other than nitrogen change solid flammability? Diluent choice for habitat air affects both flammability and suppression. No solid-fuel test with CO2 or helium diluents.

docs.title: Q15 · Which materials burn in a suit atmosphere of 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi, at lunar gravity?
docs.text: Which materials burn in a suit atmosphere of 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi, at lunar gravity? Suit and suitport materials face the most oxygen-rich environment on a mission. Complete absence of data.

docs.title: Q16 · How quickly does a fire in a sealed module deplete oxygen enough to put itself out?
docs.text: How quickly does a fire in a sealed module deplete oxygen enough to put itself out? Determines whether isolating a module is a viable fire response. Small chambers only; no module-scale depletion curve.

docs.title: Q17 · What ventilation speed minimises fire risk in a habitat module?
docs.text: What ventilation speed minimises fire risk in a habitat module? Too little flow and smoke pools; too much and a fire is fed. Designers need the safe band. The band where fires are least likely has not been defined for thick materials at habitat oxygen.

docs.title: Q18 · How does the low-flow quenching limit change with sample thickness?
docs.text: How does the low-flow quenching limit change with sample thickness? Thick materials dominate the real fuel load of a cabin. No single-material thickness series at fixed flow direction.

docs.title: Q19 · When does a downstream (concurrent) flame become viable under microgravity ventilation?
docs.text: When does a downstream (concurrent) flame become viable under microgravity ventilation? Downstream flames grow fastest; knowing their threshold sets a ventilation ceiling. Threshold not measured for thick fuels or at habitat oxygen.

docs.title: Q20 · Why did the opposed-flow SAFFIRE-I burn last 70 s while the concurrent one lasted 420 s?
docs.text: Why did the opposed-flow SAFFIRE-I burn last 70 s while the concurrent one lasted 420 s? Flow direction may change fire duration by a factor of six at large scale. The table does not record why S2 ended or how far it spread.

docs.title: Q21 · What happens to an established flame when ventilation is switched off and back on?
docs.text: What happens to an established flame when ventilation is switched off and back on? Fans cycle and fail; a flame that revives when flow returns is a hidden hazard. No flight test restores ventilation after an apparent extinction, so re-ignition in orbit is unmeasured.

docs.title: Q22 · Is a flame on the end of an object (stagnation flow) more stable than one spreading along it?
docs.text: Is a flame on the end of an object (stagnation flow) more stable than one spreading along it? Pipe ends, cable ends and corners face oncoming flow. Stagnation and parallel-flow limits not compared on one material.

docs.title: Q23 · How do wire bundles and cable insulation burn in microgravity?
docs.text: How do wire bundles and cable insulation burn in microgravity? Electrical faults are the most likely ignition source in a spacecraft. Complete absence of data in this dataset.

docs.title: Q24 · How do foams and packaging materials burn in microgravity?
docs.text: How do foams and packaging materials burn in microgravity? Cargo bags and foams make up a large share of the combustible mass in a module. Complete absence of data in this dataset.

docs.title: Q25 · How do circuit boards and electronics enclosures burn?
docs.text: How do circuit boards and electronics enclosures burn? Electronics combine an ignition source with polymer fuel. Complete absence of data in this dataset.

docs.title: Q26 · Why did Nomex fail to ignite while the PMMA attached to it burned completely?
docs.text: Why did Nomex fail to ignite while the PMMA attached to it burned completely? Real assemblies mix materials; one burning material may or may not ignite its neighbour. One sample; the heat transfer between the two was not measured.

docs.title: Q27 · Is silicone's reversal (burns at 1 g, barely in microgravity) real away from its oxygen limit?
docs.text: Is silicone's reversal (burns at 1 g, barely in microgravity) real away from its oxygen limit? If silicone is safer in space only near the limit, the advantage may vanish at habitat oxygen. Only four samples, all near the oxygen limit.

docs.title: Q28 · Do thick materials reach steady flame spread in microgravity within available test times?
docs.text: Do thick materials reach steady flame spread in microgravity within available test times? Thick materials dominate the fuel load but are slow to reach steady burning. Steady-state data for thick materials is sparse.

docs.title: Q29 · Does lunar dust on a surface change how it ignites or burns?
docs.text: Does lunar dust on a surface change how it ignites or burns? Dust will coat everything in a lunar habitat. No flammability test with dust-covered samples.

docs.title: Q30 · Why did so many diluted-butane ignition attempts fail in CFI-G?
docs.text: Why did so many diluted-butane ignition attempts fail in CFI-G? Ignition failures mark the edge of flammability, the most informative region. The CFI-G table does not separate igniter problems from true non-flammability.

docs.title: Q31 · What ignition energy does a solid need at habitat oxygen levels?
docs.text: What ignition energy does a solid need at habitat oxygen levels? Sets how hot a fault must get to start a fire. No measured minimum ignition energy for solids in microgravity.

docs.title: Q32 · Why do flames self-extinguish at steady airflow in microgravity?
docs.text: Why do flames self-extinguish at steady airflow in microgravity? A flame that dies on its own without intervention changes how a crew should respond. The cause (oxygen depletion, heat loss, fuel geometry) is not separated.

docs.title: Q33 · At what droplet size does radiation put out a flame?
docs.text: At what droplet size does radiation put out a flame? Large spills burn differently from small droplets. Radiative extinction has not been isolated from other causes in the table.

docs.title: Q34 · Can a near-limit flame relight when oxygen or airflow recovers?
docs.text: Can a near-limit flame relight when oxygen or airflow recovers? Determines whether a fire that seems out must still be monitored. No microgravity flight data on relight after near-limit burning.

docs.title: Q35 · What does aged smoke from FLAMING materials look like in microgravity?
docs.text: What does aged smoke from FLAMING materials look like in microgravity? Smoke detectors are tuned to particle sizes; flaming smoke differs from heated-sample smoke. No microgravity smoke data from real flames.

docs.title: Q36 · Can smoke detectors tell lunar dust from smoke?
docs.text: Can smoke detectors tell lunar dust from smoke? False alarms erode trust; missed fires are worse. No test exposed a detector to dust and smoke together.

docs.title: Q37 · Which sensor detects an invisible cool flame first?
docs.text: Which sensor detects an invisible cool flame first? A cool flame gives off little light, so optical detectors may miss it. No comparison of CO, formaldehyde or infrared sensors on cool flames.

docs.title: Q38 · How quickly does carbon monoxide build up before a fire is visible?
docs.text: How quickly does carbon monoxide build up before a fire is visible? CO is both a hazard and a detection signal. Only start and end values; no time history in the table.

docs.title: Q39 · Does smoke aging time change where detectors should be placed?
docs.text: Does smoke aging time change where detectors should be placed? Smoke particles grow as they drift; a detector far from a fire sees different smoke. Link between aging, distance and detector response not established.

docs.title: Q40 · Can radiometers give earlier warning than smoke detectors?
docs.text: Can radiometers give earlier warning than smoke detectors? Radiant heat may be detectable before smoke reaches a sensor. No comparison of radiometer and smoke-detector timing.

docs.title: Q41 · How well does CO2 put out solid fires at reduced pressure and raised oxygen?
docs.text: How well does CO2 put out solid fires at reduced pressure and raised oxygen? CO2 extinguishers are standard on spacecraft; their margin at habitat conditions is unknown. No solid-fire suppression data in microgravity at habitat conditions.

docs.title: Q42 · Is helium a better suppressant than CO2 at the same concentration?
docs.text: Is helium a better suppressant than CO2 at the same concentration? Suppressant choice affects mass, toxicity and effectiveness. No controlled comparison at matched oxygen and pressure.

docs.title: Q43 · Does water mist work in microgravity?
docs.text: Does water mist work in microgravity? Water is plentiful and non-toxic. Complete absence of data in this dataset.

docs.title: Q44 · Can cutting ventilation be used to put out a fire without filling the cabin with smoke?
docs.text: Can cutting ventilation be used to put out a fire without filling the cabin with smoke? Turning off fans starves a microgravity flame but stops smoke removal. Smoke distribution after ventilation shutdown is unmeasured.

docs.title: Q45 · How is a module's atmosphere recovered after a fire?
docs.text: How is a module's atmosphere recovered after a fire? Post-fire cleanup decides whether a module can be re-entered. Recovery time and scrubber load are not in PSI.

docs.title: Q46 · Why did cool flames appear only in one fuel and pressure in CFI-G?
docs.text: Why did cool flames appear only in one fuel and pressure in CFI-G? Knowing where cool flames occur tells designers where to look for them. Other fuels and pressures produced none in this table; the reason is not established.

docs.title: Q47 · Can vapours from heated cabin materials form cool flames?
docs.text: Can vapours from heated cabin materials form cool flames? An overheating material might burn invisibly before visible flame appears. No cool-flame test with pyrolysis vapours from solids.

docs.title: Q48 · Do large heptane spills create a cool-flame hazard?
docs.text: Do large heptane spills create a cool-flame hazard? Liquid hydrocarbons are carried as fuels and solvents. The FLEX table records visible extinction only.

docs.title: Q49 · How does a fire grow from glovebox scale to module scale?
docs.text: How does a fire grow from glovebox scale to module scale? Small tests are cheap; real fires are large. Few intermediate scales to connect the two.

docs.title: Q50 · What heat release rate does a realistic module fire produce?
docs.text: What heat release rate does a realistic module fire produce? Sets the load on cooling and suppression systems. No heat release data in the PSI tables.

docs.title: Q51 · How long can a large fire burn in a sealed spacecraft?
docs.text: How long can a large fire burn in a sealed spacecraft? Determines how much time a crew has. Duration vs volume and oxygen not characterised.

docs.title: Q52 · How did each BASS (PSI-26) test end, and under what conditions?
docs.text: How did each BASS (PSI-26) test end, and under what conditions? BASS has 122 tests whose outcomes would double the solid-fuel evidence. No oxygen, airflow or outcome in the experimental table.

docs.title: Q53 · What pressure did each solid-fuel test run at?
docs.text: What pressure did each solid-fuel test run at? Without pressure, reduced-pressure risk cannot be read from existing data. Pressure missing for all 300+ solid tests.

docs.title: Q54 · What does the FLEX-2 per-test data show?
docs.text: What does the FLEX-2 per-test data show? FLEX-2 extends droplet work to more fuels and mixtures. Per-test FLEX-2 results are not in this dataset.

docs.text: Do not approve habitat materials on the Earth upward-burning test alone. Add a microgravity or low-flow test for any material that will fill a habitat, because the normal-gravity screening test can misjudge it in both directions. docs.title: R2 · Test materials at the habitat's own atmosphere before choosing 30% oxygen
docs.text: Test materials at the habitat's own atmosphere before choosing 30% oxygen. Run flammability tests at about 30% O2 and 70 kPa, and use the Saffire V-VI results, before fixing the habitat atmosphere. No solid fuel in the PSI tables was tested above 22.2% O2, and no solid-fuel table records pressure. Saffire V and VI burned samples at 26.2-31.0% O2 and 54-71 kPa in Cygnus, close to habitat conditions

docs.title: R4 · Shut off ventilation to fight a fire, and confirm it is fully out before turning it back on
docs.text: Shut off ventilation to fight a fire, and confirm it is fully out before turning it back on. Make it possible to stop air movement quickly in each module, and before ventilation is restored, check that no near-invisible flamelets survive; do not treat slow air as safe. docs.title: R5 · Qualify smoke detectors with real flaming smoke and lunar dust
docs.text: Qualify smoke detectors with real flaming smoke and lunar dust. Test habitat detectors against smoke from flaming materials and against lunar dust, not only heated-sample smoke. docs.text: SIBAL: A cotton-fiberglass fabric used as a standard test fuel. The name comes from the earlier project it was made for.

docs.title: Nomex
docs.text: Nomex: A fire-barrier fabric used widely on the ISS.

docs.title: Pot (fan pot)
docs.text: Pot (fan pot): The potentiometer setting of the BASS-II fan: the knob that set the airflow. Airflow speeds on this site are converted from the fan's Air display reading with NASA's calibration (velocity = Air display × 1.0066 cm/s).

docs.title: Opposed flow
docs.text: Opposed flow: Air moving against the direction the flame spreads (the flame spreads upwind).

docs.title: Concurrent flow
docs.text: Concurrent flow: Air moving in the same direction the flame spreads (the flame spreads downwind), as in Earth's upward-burning Test 1.

docs.title: Stagnation flow
docs.text: Stagnation flow: Air flowing straight at the end of a rod, so the flame sits on the rod's tip like a cap.

docs.title: Quenching extinction
docs.text: Quenching extinction: A flame going out because the airflow is too weak to feed it.

docs.title: Blowoff
docs.text: Blowoff: A flame going out because the airflow is too strong.

docs.title: Flamelets
docs.text: Flamelets: Small separate flames that a starved flame front breaks into; each burns its own channel toward the incoming air.

docs.title: MSG
docs.text: MSG: The Microgravity Science Glovebox, the sealed workspace on the ISS where BASS and BASS-II burned their samples.

docs.id: On the NASA KC-135 aircraft, thin cellul
docs.title: Upward Flame Spread Over Thin Solids in Partial Gravity
docs.text: On the NASA KC-135 aircraft, thin cellulose samples (1, 2 and 4 cm wide) burned upward in air at 0.2-0.4 atm at 0.10 g, 0.16 g (lunar) and 0.38 g (martian). Steady spread speeds and pyrolysis lengths were approximately proportional to the gravity level.

docs.title: Most Probable Fire Scenarios in Spacecraft and Extraterrestrial Habitats - Why NASA's Current Test 1 Might Not Always Be Conservative
docs.text: For a cellulose fuel in opposed flow, the limiting oxygen index on Earth is 16.5% O2, but with flow on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s) flames can be sustained at 14% O2.

docs.text: Plastic cylinders burned aboard Mir did not spread along the rod as intended; the flame stabilized at the front tip of the rod and burned like a candle flame at the end of a fat wick.

docs.title: Most Probable Fire Scenarios in Spacecraft and Extraterrestrial Habitats - Why NASA's Current Test 1 Might Not Always Be Conservative
docs.text: Flames in microgravity preferentially spread upwind (opposed flow), not downwind as in the normal-gravity upward screening Test 1.

docs.title: Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity
docs.text: Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested lunar gravity could be more hazardous, since flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks there; related work suggests the oxygen concentration needed for flammability reaches a minimum near lunar gravity.

docs.title: Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity
docs.text: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2), planned for launch in late 2026, will burn four solid fuel samples in quiescent habitable atmospheres in real lunar gravity, with cameras, radiometers and an oxygen sensor.

docs.id: Near extinction, in weakly convective en
docs.title: New Species of Fire Discovered: Fingering Flamelets Form a Dynamic Population
docs.text: Near extinction, in weakly convective environments such as microgravity or in vertically confined spaces, a flame breaks into numerous flamelets that form a fingering pattern as they spread across the fuel. This extends the flammability range to lower opposed flow velocities, lower oxygen concentrations or higher heat loss.

docs.id: US spacecraft crews turn off ventilation
docs.title: New Species of Fire Discovered: Fingering Flamelets Form a Dynamic Population
docs.text: US spacecraft crews turn off ventilation to help put out a fire, then reactivate it to clear the smoke. Some flamelets can survive, and NASA Glenn experiments demonstrated that flamelets quickly grow into a large fire when ventilation increases.
